explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. David says the LORD "trains my hands for war, my fingers for battle." (Psalm 144:1) Notice who the trainer is. David doesn't brag about his own skills, he gives the credit to his Rock. I've pressed thousands of cookies and I'd never claim my mustache learned it alone.

Good guess, since farms and buildings do show up later in this psalm. But here David says the LORD trains his hands "for war" and his fingers "for battle." (Psalm 144:1) Farming and building aren't in that verse. Those hands are getting ready for a fight, and the LORD is the one doing the training.

Nice, careful hands do come to mind, and I respect a good stitch. But David says the LORD trains his hands "for war" and his fingers "for battle." (Psalm 144:1) No needles in this verse, friend. This is a king talking about the fight, and about who trained him for it.

That's it. David says the LORD is "my shield, in whom I take refuge." (Psalm 144:2) Taking refuge means running TO something safe. When the dough gets scary, I'd like a big strong oven mitt, and David picked a much better place to hide.

Close, because a shield does sound like guard duty. But David says he takes refuge in Him. (Psalm 144:2) Guarding is the shield's job in a way, but David's own part here is hiding behind it. Nobody asked him to stand there with a flashlight.

Keeping watch is a fine thing to do, and plenty of folks stay up late doing it. But David says the LORD is "my shield, in whom I take refuge." (Psalm 144:2) He isn't pacing the walls with a lantern. He's tucked in behind the shield, safe.

explanations.answer: Why He would think of man
explanations.explanation: You got it. David asks, "O LORD, what is man, that You regard him, the son of man that You think of him?" (Psalm 144:3) He's looking at how big the LORD is and how small we are, and he's amazed that the LORD thinks of us at all. I think that's a good place to land after all that talk of fortresses.

explanations.answer: Why He made man at all
explanations.explanation: That's a thoughtful guess, and it's close to the neighborhood. But David asks why the LORD "regards" man and "thinks of" him. (Psalm 144:3) He isn't asking why people were made. He's amazed that the LORD pays attention to us at all.

I see where that came from, since this psalm has some big, stormy asks coming. But in verse 3, David asks, "what is man, that You regard him, the son of man that You think of him?" (Psalm 144:3) Nothing about a judging day there. It's wonder, plain and simple.

Right. David asks, "Flash forth Your lightning and scatter them; shoot Your arrows and rout them." (Psalm 144:6) To rout someone means to beat them so they run. David is asking the LORD for a full win, and he's asking Him for it, not trying to do it himself.

A warning shot would be polite, I'll give you that. But David says "scatter them" and "rout them." (Psalm 144:6) Lightning and arrows aren't a gentle note on the door. This is David asking for them to be beaten.

That's a kind thought, baker, and I like the heart behind it. But the verse says "scatter them" and "rout them." (Psalm 144:6) Arrows aren't how you lead anybody to safety. David is praying for these enemies to be defeated.

Not quite, friend. David describes these foreigners as people "whose mouths speak falsehood, whose right hands are deceitful." (Psalm 144:8) So their words are false, not true. Their right hands are deceitful too, so you couldn't even trust a handshake.

Yes, false. David says the foreigners' "mouths speak falsehood, whose right hands are deceitful." (Psalm 144:8) So they speak lies, not truth. And he says their right hands are deceitful, so even a handshake from them can't be trusted.

That's the one. David says, "I will sing to You a new song, O God; on a harp of ten strings I will make music to You." (Psalm 144:9) He's still asking for rescue, and he stops to sing anyway. That's a lot of music for someone in a tight spot.
A temple would be a big gift, I'll give you that. But in Psalm 144:9, David says, "I will sing to You a new song, O God." A song, not a building project. No blueprints, just a harp and a voice.

Good thinking, since altars come up all over the Bible. But here David says, "I will sing to You a new song, O God." (Psalm 144:9) No stones to stack in this verse. He's bringing music, and he even names the instrument.

True. David sings to "Him who gives victory to kings, who frees His servant David from the deadly sword." (Psalm 144:10) Notice he calls himself the LORD's servant, even though he's a king. The song goes to the One who rescues, and that's who gets the thank-you.

Not this time, friend. Right after he promises the song, David says it's for "Him who gives victory to kings, who frees His servant David from the deadly sword." (Psalm 144:10) So the statement is true. The song is for the One who gives the victory.

You got it. David says, "Then our sons will be like plants nurtured in their youth." (Psalm 144:12) Think of a plant that gets watered and looked after while it's young. That's the picture, and it's a sweet one.

Good guess, but servants aren't in this verse. David says, "our sons will be like plants nurtured in their youth." (Psalm 144:12) It's the sons who get the plant picture. Watered and cared for from the start.

I can see why you'd pick that, since a plant that's grown tall sounds wise. But David says "our sons will be like plants nurtured in their youth." (Psalm 144:12) The word "youth" gives it away. These are the young ones, getting cared for as they grow.

Right. David says, "our daughters like corner pillars carved to adorn a palace." (Psalm 144:12) Corner pillars hold up a building and look beautiful doing it. That's a picture of strength and beauty together.

A gate is a solid guess, since this psalm is full of walls and defense. But David says the pillars are "carved to adorn a palace." (Psalm 144:12) Carved pillars, fancy ones, the kind you'd find in a king's home.

Nice try, since towers are a strong image. But David says the corner pillars are "carved to adorn a palace." (Psalm 144:12) A watchtower is built to keep watch. These pillars are carved to be beautiful in a palace.
Yes. David says, "There will be no breach in the walls." (Psalm 144:14) A breach is a gap where enemies could break in. In his picture, every wall stays whole, with no hole anywhere.
Gold gates would look great, I admit. But David says, "There will be no breach in the walls." (Psalm 144:14) He isn't picturing fancy gates. He's picturing walls that nobody breaks through.

That sounds impressive, baker, but it isn't in the verse. David says, "There will be no breach in the walls." (Psalm 144:14) The point isn't how tall the walls are. A breach is a gap, and in his picture there isn't one.
Not quite, friend. David's picture says the opposite. He says there will be "no going into captivity." (Psalm 144:14) Nobody gets carried off in this picture. Everyone stays home.

Correct, it's false. David says there will be "no breach in the walls, no going into captivity, and no cry of lament in our streets." (Psalm 144:14) Nobody is taken away in his picture, and the people stay safe at home.

That's the word. David ends with, "Blessed are the people of whom this is so; blessed are the people whose God is the LORD." (Psalm 144:15) He opened the psalm with "Blessed be the LORD," and he closes on blessed too. It starts and ends in the same good place.

I know it's a tempting word, but it doesn't fit this ending. David says, "Blessed are the people of whom this is so; blessed are the people whose God is the LORD." (Psalm 144:15) Forgotten is a word from the drawer days, not from David's closing line. He calls them blessed, twice.

Scattered shows up earlier, when David asks the LORD to "scatter them" about his enemies. (Psalm 144:6) But he ends the psalm with a different word for God's people. "Blessed are the people of whom this is so; blessed are the people whose God is the LORD." (Psalm 144:15)
